question: What do we call a disease that is always present at a steady, expected level in a specific area?
explanation: Think of an endemic disease as having a permanent, predictable home in a certain region over time. You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h1)

question: How is an outbreak different from an epidemic?

options.A: An epidemic is restricted strictly to hospital environments.
options.B: An outbreak usually covers a smaller, more localized geographic area.
options.C: An epidemic never involves more than ten total infected people.
options.D: An outbreak only involves non-communicable chronic conditions.

explanation: Outbreaks are usually small and contained to a specific community, whereas epidemics spread much wider and affect more people. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h1)

question: Which type of germ is usually behind a sudden outbreak of waterborne stomach illness?
explanation: When drinking water gets contaminated, harmful bacteria and viruses easily find their way in and cause stomach upsets. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h2)

question: A nurse notices a sudden jump in malaria cases during the rainy season. What kind of transmission is this?
explanation: Spot on! Malaria is spread by mosquitoes (the vector), which love to breed in the puddles formed during the rainy season. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h2)

question: Why do healthcare workers set a clear 'case definition' during a disease outbreak?

options.A: To immediately eliminate the infectious agent from the environment
options.B: To replace laboratory testing with simple clinical guesses
options.C: To ensure all healthcare workers count cases using identical criteria
options.D: To determine the financial cost of treating infected patients

explanation: A case definition gives everyone the same checklist so that all nurses and doctors are counting and reporting the exact same illness accurately. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h3)

question: Which of these is normally NOT needed when creating a standard case definition for a disease?
explanation: Disease tracking is about clinical signs, time, and place—a person's religion has nothing to do with how an infection spreads! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h3)

question: What is the main benefit of drawing an epidemic curve during an investigation?

options.A: It automatically cures infected patients within the first week.
options.B: It replaces the need for laboratory confirmation of blood samples.
options.C: It helps show how the disease is spreading and when exposure likely happened.
options.D: It proves which specific nurse made the initial error.

explanation: An epidemic curve is simply a graph of symptom timelines. It helps investigators spot patterns and figure out when people first caught the illness. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h4)

question: What is the first thing a community health nurse should do when an unusual cluster of sick people appears?

options.A: Wait several months to see if the symptoms disappear on their own
options.B: Organize an international press conference in the capital city
options.C: Verify the diagnosis and confirm that an outbreak is actually occurring
options.D: Close all schools and markets in the entire country permanently

explanation: Before sounding any alarms, always confirm your facts and verify the diagnosis first. Good nursing practice! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h4)

question: What is the main difference between quarantine and isolation?

options.A: Quarantine restricts people who were exposed but are not yet sick, while isolation separates those who are already confirmed sick.
options.B: Quarantine involves giving preventive medications, while isolation involves performing major surgical procedures.
options.C: Quarantine is only used for waterborne diseases, whereas isolation is reserved exclusively for vector-borne illnesses.
options.D: Quarantine takes place in private homes, while isolation can only happen in national research laboratories.

explanation: Easy way to remember: Isolation is for those who are already sick, while quarantine is for those who were exposed and are waiting to see if they fall ill. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h5)

question: Which of these actions directly targets the environmental cause of a waterborne disease?
explanation: Chlorine cleans the water supply, stopping harmful germs right at the source before they reach anyone's cup. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h5)

question: A nurse wants to teach a rural community how to prevent cholera. What is the best way to communicate?

options.A: Distribute dense medical textbooks written in advanced technical English.
options.B: Post warning notices exclusively on international websites.
options.C: Use local languages and collaborate with respected community leaders.
options.D: Rely entirely on unspoken signs posted without any translation.

explanation: People listen best to trusted community voices speaking in their own language. Communication is key in public health! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h6)

question: What is a major goal of community mobilization when responding to an outbreak?

options.A: Encouraging citizens to avoid primary health clinics entirely
options.B: Punishing individuals who fall ill with the infectious disease
options.C: Empowering residents to adopt safe hygiene and sanitation practices
options.D: Eliminating the need for any future environmental sanitation

explanation: When communities are involved and empowered, they take charge of their own hygiene, making disease prevention much easier. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h6)
